definition: Of, relating to, or occurring at perigee — the point in the moon's (or any orbiting body's) path when it is nearest to the Earth. Perigean tides are noticeably higher than ordinary tides, pulled by the moon's closer gravitational grip.
etymology: From Greek peri, meaning 'around' or 'near,' plus gaia, meaning 'earth' — so the full root means 'near the earth.' Greek astronomers coined perigaion to name this closest approach, and the word passed through medieval Latin into the languages of European astronomy just as scholars were learning to track the moon's elliptical wandering with real precision.
usage: November's full moon, rising vast and amber over the estuary, happened to be perigean, and the night fishermen watched the tide climb the harbour wall a full foot higher than the almanac had promised.
